props.title: End of Days
props.initialSlug: A former cop protects a woman targeted by Satan

sections.content: End of Days marked a fascinating shift in millennial anxiety horror, arriving as Y2K paranoia peaked. Arnold Schwarzenegger's rare foray into supernatural horror sees him battling Satan himself in New York City. The film follows similar religious horror beats as The Omen (1976) and The Exorcist (1973), but adds explosive action sequences and apocalyptic stakes. Director Peter Hyams blends late 90s CGI spectacle with practical effects, creating a darker tone than Schwarzenegger's typical fare.

sections.content: The late 90s saw a surge in religious horror-action hybrids, reflecting pre-millennium tensions. The Ninth Gate (1999) explored rare book dealing and devil worship, while Lost Souls (2000) continued the possession narrative into the new millennium. These films marked a distinct evolution from the more grounded 70s religious horror classics, incorporating modern special effects and action elements to attract wider audiences.

Schwarzenegger's performance represents a significant departure from his established action persona. Unlike Total Recall (1990) or True Lies (1994), his character Jericho Cane is vulnerable and haunted, dealing with faith and loss rather than just physical threats. This character complexity, though sometimes overshadowed by explosive set pieces, shows Hollywood's attempts to merge serious theological themes with commercial action formulas. movies.slug: A detective discovers a supernatural entity that can leap from person to person through touch

sections.content: The film's impact on subsequent religious-themed action horror remains notable. Legion (2010) borrowed its warriors-versus-supernatural-evil premise, while Priest (2011) adapted similar themes to a post-apocalyptic setting. End of Days established a template for mixing theological horror with high-budget action sequences, influencing everything from Van Helsing (2004) to Season of the Witch (2011).
